While trendy desserts like cupcakes, macarons, and whoopie pies continue to gain attention, Britain remains a nation of biscuit lovers, especially when it comes to afternoon snacks. The average household consumes a(n) [[1]] 103 packets of biscuits per year. As fancy patisseries pop up everywhere with cake stands piled high, this humble teatime tradition holds firm: biscuits are the [[2]] for casual gatherings and quick tea breaks. Whether it’s dunking a whole bourbon cream in tea or savoring its layers [[3]], everyone has a favorite.
In contrast to their popularity and omnipresence today, biscuits, [[4]], weren’t always such a beloved treat. Historically, they were simple flour-and-water rations for sailors and soldiers—a(n) [[5]] way of preserving carbohydrates. Over time, they evolved into sponge cake-like creations, dried in ovens—hence the name “biscuit,” meaning “twice-baked” in French. By the 18th century, these sponge fingers were often dipped in sweet wine, much like Italy’s Cantucci e Vin Santo (almond biscotti dunked in wine). It wasn’t until the 19th century, with the [[6]] of afternoon tea, that biscuits became synonymous with tea-drinking. This uniquely British tradition has since spread worldwide while still deeply ingrained in the national diet. Despite increasing concerns over health and sugar [[7]], biscuit sales have stayed strong, even growing slightly in recent years. While healthier [[8]] like cereal bars are gaining traction, classic biscuits, such as digestives, top the nation’s list of favorites, with 4.4 million consumed daily.
Though Britain is not entirely resistant to change—new products are being launched from time to time—nostalgia plays a major role in biscuit [[9]]. Customers often develop an attachment to their favorite biscuits early in life, pledging eternal loyalty. Even recipe changes, like McVitie’s 2009 reduction of saturated fat, could [[10]] heated debate, thus proving one thing: in Britain, biscuits truly matter.
